Every sample bag we send out carries a story before it carries a flavor — the farm, the altitude, the processing choices behind the cup. This is that story, kept current for the lots we’re currently offering.

5 origins on file Source: grower & importer lot documentation

🇧🇷  Brazil

Diamond

Diamond is blended across a wide base of Minas Gerais farms to hold the same cup, harvest after harvest. It leans neutral and smooth — a coffee built to disappear into a blend rather than announce itself, which is exactly the point: a dependable foundation for drip or espresso that customers keep coming back to.

Reading the grade

NY2 means no more than 4 full-defect equivalents in a 200g sample. Screen 17/18 is the second-largest bean size, 6.75–7mm — large and even enough to roast the whole lot to one level. “SS” is strictly soft: a stable, clean cup.

🇧🇷  Brazil

Santos NY2 Scr. 17/18 FC Natural

The name predates the grading system that replaced it — before the 1990s, Brazilian export lots were simply Santos 1, Santos 2, Santos 3, named for the port that shipped them out. The port name stuck because the quality did: sweet, smooth, medium-bodied, with a creamy, mellow cup that reads as immediately familiar.

Reading the grade

Here NY2 allows up to 6 full-defect equivalents per 300g sample — still a clean, consistent cup, just graded on a slightly larger reference sample than the Diamond lot above. “FC” is fine cup: a clean, unremarkable defect profile.

🇨🇷  Costa Rica

Hacienda Sonora — Caturra Natural

Hacienda Sonora sits at the foot of the Poás Volcano, 100 hectares farmed by Diego Guardia and run on renewable power — a hydroelectric generator turns the rivers on the property into electricity for the wet and dry mills, and for every house on the farm. Only 45 of those hectares carry coffee; the rest is forest reserve and a 150-year-old sugarcane planting.

On the record

Sonora reports its carbon numbers to NAMA Café de Costa Rica, the country’s first climate-mitigation program for coffee, and gets a share of its own carbon-reduction investment back. Caturra itself is a natural dwarf mutation of Bourbon, first found in Minas Gerais around 1915 — smaller plants, higher density, and a cup that leans floral and fruity.

🇭🇳  Honduras

COMSA — SHG EP Organic FW

Café Orgánico Marcala Sociedad Anónima started in 2001 with 69 farmers. It now works with more than 1,200, most farming under two hectares, and has become a reference point for organic, cooperative coffee production across Central America — training members, producing its own organic inputs, and reinvesting in the community around Marcala.

Beyond the cup

COMSA runs a recycling plant serving 44 schools in Marcala, keeps a beekeeping program for members, and in 2017 turned a failing private school into the COMSA International School — dual-language, Montessori-influenced, 80–90% of students on scholarship. Their model farm, Finca La Fortaleza, trains cooperatives from across the region.

🇳🇮  Nicaragua

Tierra Madre Mujeres — FW RA Organic

Behind this lot are 125 women coffee producers in Jinotega, members of Asociación Aldea Global’s Tierra Madre program. In a region where women hold only 15% of land titles, the program pays these producers an additional premium for meeting a high quality standard — a premium built specifically to help them fund the legal titling of their own land.

What the certifications mean

Rainforest Alliance requires at least 40% canopy cover, 12+ native tree species per hectare on average, and vegetation buffers around water — on top of the Organic certification these farms also hold. Aldea Global itself started in 1992 with 22 members on the shores of Lake Apanás and has since grown to several thousand.
